significance: The second-largest Buddhist temple compound in Indonesia, named Manjusrigrha, the house of Manjushri, in an inscription of about 792; work began under Rakai Panangkaran and was completed under King Indra. Its 249 shrines are set out as a mandala representing the universe, and it was the kingdom's chief Buddhist sanctuary before Borobudur and Prambanan rose nearby. Volcanic debris buried the site, which was rediscovered early in the nineteenth century, looted during the Java War, photographed by 1867 and systematically reconstructed from 1908.
story: Local folklore held that the temples were raised in a single night by a host of demons commanded by Bandung Bondowoso, part of the Loro Jonggrang legend attached to nearby Prambanan.
